subject: Cluster sampling design with point transects

messages.subject: Cluster sampling design with point transects
parts:
Hi all, 

 

Following is a question related to cluster sampling design for which I would like to ask your advice since I was not able to find anything similar to our situation in the design sections of general distance sampling books (Buckland et al. 1993; Strindberg et al. 2004; Buckland et al. 2015) and specialised primate sections (Peres, 1999; Buckland et al. 2010; Ross and Reeve 2011).

 

Context

I have the opportunity to join a team currently conducting a bird survey in a forested national park in the Philippines, in order to conduct a separate macaque population survey while benefiting from their logistics. This is in an area where we know little about the primates. However, this situation also means that my survey is restricted by their plan, and I am having doubts about the most efficient design to adopt within their conditions. 

 

Planning

  • The survey will be conducted from bivouac camps in the park, during week-long expeditions comprising 2 camps each. 
  • For the location of the camps, they made a grid of 2,5 km-wide squares in the middle of which the camps will be set. The blue dots represent the camp locations which were randomly chosen, yet I will only be able to access 8-10 of them in the time of the study (4-5 expeditions). The camps visited are still to be confirmed, but chosen indenpendantly from the terrain.
  • In each camp we will stay 2 days surveying points equally spaced (every 250m) along 1 km line transects spreading out from the camp (starting at 250m from the camp).

 

As of today, I plan to follow their methodology, i.e. doing point counts every 250m on 1 km transect outward from the camps (in a cross pattern). Yet, I wonder if this design will allow to draw inferences to estimate reliable density and abundance for the whole park. According to Buckland et al. (2015:16) “If the separation of neighbouring points on the same line is less than the separation of neighbouring points on different lines, then this should be treated as cluster sampling, where each line represents one cluster of points.” 

 

My main question is the following:

Is there a problem to consider the 2 or more lines of points departing 250m from a same camp (to avoid human disturbance bias and overlapping) as independent sampling units? Would using this sampling design above respect the principles of survey design? 


Considering the different point transects from one camp together as one sampling unit would maybe produce data-rich samples but insufficient in number (8-10) for adequate replication, right? 


Thanks for your help,

Gaspard 


Ps: please pardon the lengthy message. The attached grid has been designed due to the absence of a trail system and accidented terrain making travel difficult.
